rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The midpoint temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Test temperature-dependent selectivity while keeping the gradient fixed, targeting the unresolved central pair. The current last peak is comfortably within 10 minutes, leaving room for subsequent slope adjustments.

The central peak pattern suggests an elution-order crossover between 40 and 50 C; cooling may separate this cluster more effectively. A slightly shallower gradient should protect the earlier close pair while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Cooling created several critical pairs, so test the upper temperature limit with the original gradient. This will establish whether heating resolves the central cluster and reveal any new selectivity crossover among earlier peaks.

Use 55 C to balance the competing temperature-sensitive pairs, with a shallower gradient to improve their separation. The observed retention window suggests this longer gradient should still place the last peak within 10 minutes.
The maximum CRF is achieved; now shorten the gradient by one step to seek a faster fully resolved method. Keep temperature and endpoints fixed to test whether the critical pair retains R >= 1.5.
Slightly reduce the gradient slope to recover resolution for the pair at R 1.47, while retaining most of the time savings from injection 6. Injection 5 remains the fully resolved fallback.

Shift the gradient window upward while preserving the slope of injection 7 to test faster elution without sacrificing full resolution. Monitor both central critical pairs; injection 7 remains the faster proven maximum-score method.

Lower the starting organic fraction to improve the pair that deteriorated in injection 8, while using a steeper gradient than injection 7 to limit late-peak retention. This tests a potentially faster fully resolved method at the established favorable temperature.

Increase the gradient slope slightly to shorten late-peak retention; previous slope tests suggest this may also improve the marginal central pair. The other critical pair has some resolution margin at this lower starting organic fraction.

Shorten the fastest proven fully resolved gradient by one grid step to test its speed limit. Both critical pairs are close to the threshold, so retain injection 10 as the maximum-score fallback if resolution deteriorates.

Test a faster, hotter gradient to move beyond the earlier central-pair crossover and potentially recover separation in reversed elution order. This explores a distinct fast-method regime while retaining injection 10 as the proven fully resolved fallback.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to test whether the unresolved pair separates further beyond its apparent crossover. Watch the first two peaks and the neighboring central pair for compression while pursuing a fully resolved run under five minutes.

Lower the starting organic fraction to protect early and neighboring central separations, while steepening the gradient to test separation beyond the temperature-sensitive crossover. This explores another fast regime without repeating a method; injection 10 remains the proven fully resolved fallback.

Test an intermediate cooler temperature for a different balance of central-pair selectivity, since the fast 60 C methods leave multiple unresolved pairs. The low starting organic fraction protects early separation, and this gradient should keep the last peak within 10 minutes.

Refine the proven 55 C region with a slope between injections 6 and 7, targeting full resolution with a last peak near 7.8 minutes. This should balance the two critical pairs better than the faster gradients while shortening the programmed gradient to 10 minutes.

Test whether a faster gradient at 40 C separates the central cluster differently from the unsuccessful 60 C regime. This offers another route to a shorter fully resolved run while retaining injection 10 as the fastest proven maximum-score method.

Narrow the gradient window and shorten its duration while preserving the slope of the fastest fully resolved method, injection 10. Because its last peak eluted at 7.60 minutes, before this gradient reaches its endpoint at the outlet, full resolution should be retained.

Test a slope of 0.080 organic fraction per minute, between the fastest fully resolved slope of 0.075 and the unsuccessful 0.090. This probes whether additional time savings are possible before the earlier critical pair falls below R = 1.5.

Test whether a shallower gradient at 60 C restores the earlier critical pair while preserving the stronger separation of the later central pair. This targets a fully resolved alternative with more resolution margin; injection 10 remains the fastest proven maximum-score method.

Return to 55 C and test whether a shallower gradient compensates for the resolution loss at a higher starting organic fraction. This probes a nearby alternative to the maximum-score methods while keeping the expected last peak below 10 minutes.

Refine the proven maximum-score region with a slope between injections 7 and 16, aiming to balance the two critical pairs with slightly greater minimum resolution. The last peak should remain comfortably below 10 minutes.

Test whether cooling to 50 C restores the earlier critical pair at a higher starting organic fraction while retaining enough separation in the later central pair. This targets a faster fully resolved alternative, with injection 10 retained as the fastest proven maximum-score method.
